s02.slug: MONDAY · 11:50 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM
body: Tomás’s record comes up through the floorboards — something new and quick, a drum that won’t sit down and a guitar skating along the top of it — loud enough in the front room that up here it’s in the mattress. On the way in he stepped around Sol’s swing on the porch: the driftwood seat lying on the boards under its two hooks, a coil of new chain beside it, not hung yet. In her room the blind is up and the window over the mattress is open on a washed, bright noon, and the light comes in white off the water and lies across the sheets.

Skye is cross-legged in the middle of the mattress in his flannel from the Walk — she never gave it back, and he never asked — and not much else, with the white iPhone in her lap. She looks up at him in the doorway, and at the Carhartt over his arm, and she is already somebody else.
“*Corinne Waxman*,” she says.

It’s all of Corinne’s hello, the name and nothing after it, and she has the vowels exactly: pleasant, rounded, immovable, a voice that has heard every objection there is and finds all of them a little sad. She takes a sip out of a coffee cup that isn’t there. “Good morning. You’re on a website. Not one of the good ones — one of the ones that would *like* to be one of the good ones. There’s a march. There’s a boy. And there is a coat.” Her eyes go to the Carhartt. “The coat is a problem, Skye. The coat has a following.”
He drops it on the floor by the door. She nods at it, satisfied, in Corinne’s face.
“Does the coat get a lawyer?” he says.
“The coat gets *managed*.”
“What do I get?”
“You,” says Corinne, kindly, with real regret, “get lunch.”

Then the rules, in Corinne’s voice, off a BlackBerry made of nothing. Every picture of the two of them comes down: hers, and anybody’s she can reach, and anybody’s she can’t reach Corinne will reach. Nothing new goes up. Not a picture. Not a status. “Not a *mood*.” And all of it — she gives the word its three syllables and a little curtsy at the end — “until we have a *strategy*.” Lunch tomorrow. Studio City. Her mother will be there. Something with sleeves.

He laughs. She’s very good. She reads him the comments in Corinne’s voice, the way Corinne would read out a ransom note in a meeting: one of them thinks he’s a Jonas Brother; one of them thinks he’s her bodyguard; one of them would very much like to know whether he is single, and has used a great many exclamation points to ask. She does a man from the network wanting to know, very gently, whether Cassidy is pro-life now, in Corinne doing the man from the network. She does the man from the network’s lawyer. She does her own mother finding out, in Corinne doing Debbie doing Corinne, and the voices go up on top of one another, each one starting before the last one has finished, and none of them stops anywhere. She’s going faster. The bit keeps finding more bit, and there’s nowhere at the bottom of it to land.
Somewhere around her mother he quits laughing. He sits down on the end of the mattress and watches her.
She’s in the middle of *strategy* again when she sees he’s stopped. The word comes apart in Corinne’s mouth halfway through, and there’s no one left in her voice to finish it.
She looks down at the phone in her lap. Downstairs the song runs out and the next one starts.
“I liked being the only thing in my life nobody wrote,” she says.
He hasn’t got anything for that that isn’t a joke, so he doesn’t give her one. He takes the phone out of her lap and sets it on the sheet behind her, out of the way.

She takes hold of the front of his shirt with both fists and pulls him down onto the mattress by it. Her mouth goes to his throat, under the hinge of the jaw, where she can feel what his pulse is doing about her, and he feels her smile at it against his skin, and his hand is on her bare thigh under the hem of the flannel — his flannel, soft from a hundred washes on Glenwood Avenue, and the skin under it warmer than the cotton. She hooks one leg over his and draws him in by it. The record changes downstairs to something; he couldn’t say what. He wants her, and at ten past noon with the blind up there is no other word in him for it: the long weight of her along his side, the freckles at the top of her shoulder where the flannel has slid off, her teeth at the cord of his neck and then her tongue where her teeth were.

His own shirt stays on. Her hands are under it, spread on his back, holding him where she wants him, and she isn’t asking for anything past that, and it doesn’t need to be anything past that to take his breath. Over her shoulder the clock on her dresser says 12:21. Hale is at one. He knows to the minute how much of the hour is left, and he would like every one of those minutes to be this.

She reaches out across the sheet without looking, finds the phone by feel, and holds it up at the end of her arm above the two of them, the back of it to the ceiling and the little lens turned down on them, blind. She can’t see what it sees. That seems to be the idea.
“Hold still,” she says, against his jaw. And then, very low, right into his ear, in Corinne’s pleasant vowels: “*A friend from school.*”
He laughs with his eyes shut — he can’t help it — and above them the phone makes its little fake shutter noise.

She brings it down and looks at it by herself. All he can see is the white back of it and her face over it, lit from underneath. She gives one short laugh through her nose at whatever’s there. Then she reaches over the edge of the mattress and lays it face down on the floorboards, on the far side of her, where he’d have to climb over her to get it.

response: “That’s for me,” she says. “I’m a strategy.”

And she does Corinne one more time, slower now, the vowels set out one at a time where she wants them — “We’ll need a strategy… for the strategy” — and this time it has a bottom to it and it lands there, and he laughs until she has to put her hand over his mouth, and he laughs into that. “I’m sorry,” Corinne says, “we’re going to need you to stop enjoying this.”

At a quarter to one she’s on her stomach with her chin on her crossed arms, watching him hunt the floor for his shoes, and she doesn’t help. One of them is under the dresser. She knew. He gets it on standing up, hopping, and goes down the stairs past Tomás’s door with the record still going, out across the porch around the swing seat, and up Del Playa toward campus with his laces untied and Tomás’s record following him half a block.
“You didn’t blink,” she says. “That’s the good one.”

She doesn’t take another. She doesn’t pick the phone up off the boards, either, or offer it to him; she lies back with her head on his arm and her eyes on the ceiling, smiling at it, as if the picture were up there. When he reaches across her for the phone anyway she catches his wrist on the way and brings his hand back to her hip, where it was, and keeps it there with hers, and that’s the end of the discussion for a while.

At a quarter to one she walks him to her door in the flannel and nothing on her feet, and reaches up and straightens his collar, carefully, with both hands. It’s a flannel collar on a Monday and he is going to a seminar on Mary Shelley, and she sets it right as if a camera were waiting for him at the bottom of the stairs. “There,” she says. “Now you look like somebody’s friend from school.” She shuts the door on him. He’s on the second step down when she opens it again, to look, and shuts it again.

choices.text: *Don’t let go of her long enough to look.*
response: He keeps both arms around her and lets the phone lie where she put it. He doesn’t ask what’s on it.

She notices. He feels her notice — she goes still against him for the length of a breath, and then her cheek comes down on his chest, over his heart, and settles. Through the flannel he can feel hers going quick against his ribs, and then less quick. Downstairs the record plays out its side, and after a while Tomás turns it over himself.
At 12:45 by the dresser clock she puts her bare foot in the middle of his back and pushes, steadily, until he rolls off the edge of the mattress onto the floorboards.
“Go argue about Frankenstein,” she says, from up on the mattress, and throws the Carhartt down on top of him.

s07.slug: TUESDAY · 10:20 AM · US-101 SOUTH, THE RINCON — THE SAAB
body: The Rincon is gray from end to end this morning: gray water, gray boulders stacked along the shoulder, a low gray lid of cloud that quits somewhere short of the islands, and out in the Channel the oil platforms standing on their legs in all of it. The top is up. Along the point the surfers sit their boards in black wetsuits, twenty or thirty of them strung out on the line, waiting on a swell that comes in long and slow out of the gray and doesn’t hurry for anybody.
Back up the coast, Dr. Fenner will take roll in Oceanography 1 at eleven and find all of Pair 41 gone. Jack’s RAZR is in his jacket with the whole morning in it. He leaves it there.

Her iPod is on: Spoon, the new record, a piano somebody is hitting with real conviction and a man singing over it like he hasn’t slept. Skye is driving in a dress her mother picked — lilac, sleeves to the wrist, a color he would bet the Saab she has never bought for herself — and her hair is up, smooth, every piece of it where it’s been told to be. Her sunglasses are pushed up into it. On the hook behind his seat hangs a garment bag with a second dress in it, in case the first one turns out to be wrong.

She’s been putting something on since Montecito, a mile at a time. At Summerland her voice still had its corners. Through Carpinteria she said *fine* about the weather, and about the lunch, and about her mother, and each time it came out a little rounder. By the Rincon it’s nearly finished: easy, warm, pleasant to the middle, a voice you could serve on a plate.
He lets her. He doesn’t say anything about the voice. He talks about the surfers instead — which ones are going to go and which ones are only out there sitting.
“Him,” he says. “Yellow board. He’s going.”
The yellow board turns and paddles and drops in late and makes it, and runs down the face toward the boulders with his arms out.
“Her. Not her. That guy’s never going.” Jack points with his chin. “That guy’s out there because his wife’s home.”
“That’s very Youngstown of you,” Skye says, in the new smooth voice, and watches the yellow board till it’s gone behind the riprap.
He asks her what her mother orders at lunch, because he’d like to know what he’s walking into.
“Oh, she’ll be fine,” Skye says. “Salad. Dressing on the side. It’ll be fine.” She says it twice, and the second one is smoother than the first, and she passes a produce truck on it.
At the county line she turns Spoon down to almost nothing and tells him about the post. He hasn’t asked.

“Corinne emailed at nine-forty last night,” she says. “She already said it on the phone at six in the morning, but Corinne likes things in an email. Subject line, *Going forward*. She cc’d my mother. Everything down. Every picture of us, mine and anybody’s. Until we have a strategy.” She checks the mirror, and changes lanes for nobody. “So I put one up.”
He’s seen it. So has his wall.
“Her own rule,” Skye says. “If anybody asks, you’re a friend from school.” The sunglasses are still up. Her eyes stay on the road. “So I put it in writing.”
A motorhome lumbers past them on the left with a bike on the back, and she waits for it to be gone.
“It wasn’t at you,” she says. “It was at them. And I didn’t ask you first.” She doesn’t dress that up. “I’m not going to say I’m sorry about that part. You’d hear me not mean it.”
They go by La Conchita, its little houses tucked up under a raw brown hill on the landward side, and the road keeps to the water. She turns Spoon off altogether.
“One rule for today,” she says. “Whatever my mother says about you — you don’t answer it. I answer it.”

body.text: “If she says anything about your brother, you’re allowed to loom. I’ve been saving that.”
“And be a wall. You’re a ten.”
“And if it gets bad, bring her a coffee. It worked on a man with a megaphone.”

body: She looks over at him then, for the first time since the county line, and leaves the music off. She hasn’t asked him what he thinks of the post.

response: She laughs. It gets out past the voice, short and surprised and entirely hers, coming up through the lilac, and he sees it surprise her.

And then she looks at him sideways for a mile anyway, checking him the way she checks a mirror before a lane change. He lets her check. There’s nothing on his face to find but what he said. “Say it like that at lunch,” she tells him finally, “and my mother will want to adopt you.” Ahead of them Ventura comes up out of the gray, the pier going out on its pilings and the brown hills standing behind the town.

choices.text: “Corinne’s going to have a stroke. I don’t care.”
response: “Everybody says they don’t care,” she says, pleasantly, to the windshield.
The sunglasses come back down. She drives on behind the dark lenses, still pleasant. “Say that to Corinne.”
“I will.”

She doesn’t answer that. He can see himself in the lenses, small and doubled, a man in a flannel saying a true thing she hasn’t got anywhere to put yet. He doesn’t say it again. People who say it twice are selling it, and she grew up on a lot full of people selling it.
The Rincon runs out behind them. Ahead the road runs on along the water toward Ventura, and the last of the surfers are only black specks on the gray, sitting.
“It’s a very good picture,” she agrees, in the smooth voice, as if they were discussing somebody else’s. “You’re in it.”
“That’s what’s good about it.”
She laughs at that, short.

At the next straightaway she checks his face — quick, sideways, the sunglasses still up — as if the answer might have changed since the last mile. It hasn’t. At the one after that she checks again. He lets her look as many times as she needs to, and keeps his eyes on the water, where another line of surfers is sitting off Mussel Shoals, waiting, and the oil island stands in the gray behind them with its palm trees, going nowhere.
